classes.title: The flat, the week, the family
classes.covered: A flat room by room and the furniture in it; the seven days of the week; the mother's side of the family and the dual; weather words around ثَلْج; and a reading passage about Samer looking for a flat.

sentences.ar: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ مِنَ الأَثَاثِ؟
sentences.en: What furniture is there in your house?
There is a table, chairs and beds.
I live in the airport neighbourhood.
Allah is Ever-Living, He does not die.
What floor is your house on?
I have a curtain for the window.
Allah is the Concealer of faults.
How many times a day do you prostrate?
This is a beautiful Pakistani carpet.

sentences.ar: الشَّقَّةُ فِيهَا غُرْفَةُ نَوْمٍ وَغُرْفَةُ جُلُوسٍ وَمَطْبَخٌ
sentences.en: The flat has a bedroom, a living room and a kitchen.

sentences.ar: مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي الشَّقَّةِ مِنَ الأَثَاثِ؟
sentences.en: What furniture is there in the flat?
In the living room there is a sofa and a chair.
We have many sofas and chairs.
In the kitchen there is a fridge and an oven.

sentences.ar: عِنْدِي خَزَانَةٌ كَبِيرَةٌ فِي غُرْفَةِ النَّوْمِ
sentences.en: I have a big cupboard in the bedroom.
The cupboards are new.
I open the window in the morning.
The mirror is in the bedroom.
The lamp is small.
My house is on the third floor.
Do you have a lift?
Today is Monday and tomorrow is Tuesday.
Wednesday is after Tuesday.
Saturday and Sunday are a holiday.
The week is seven days.
On Tuesday I go to the lesson.
The weather is cold and there is snow.
The rain comes down from the clouds.
The sun is hot and the wind is cold.
My sister is in the house.
My uncle and my aunt are from my mother's side.
This is my sister's husband.
His wife is a teacher.

grammar.why: The spine of the whole class — عِنْدِي / عِنْدَكُمْ, and both ways to negate it (مَا عِنْدِي, لَيْسَ عِنْدِي), which she gave together.
grammar.name: عِنْدَ — having, and not having

grammar.why: Her board question مَاذَا يُوجَدُ فِي بَيْتِكَ مِنَ الأَثَاثِ؟ — the way Arabic says 'there is'.
grammar.name: يُوجَدُ — there is, there are

grammar.why: خَالَانِ وَخَالَتَانِ. Arabic counts one, two, and many; the ـَانِ ending IS the two.
grammar.name: the dual — Arabic's word for exactly two

grammar.why: غُرْفَةُ نَوْمٍ, غُرْفَةُ الجُلُوسِ — two nouns pushed together with no word for 'of'. Already on the site; this class is where it earns its keep in everyday speech.
grammar.name: idafa — possession by pairing

grammar.why: مَا and لَيْسَ, as she used them with عِنْدَ.
grammar.name: the four ways to say 'not'

notes: أَرَادَ أَنْ + present (أَرَادَ أَنْ يَبْحَثَ — 'he wanted to look for') runs through the passage.
Floors are ordinals: الدَّوْر الثَّالِث, the third floor.
Feminine agreement carries the whole description of the flat: الشَّقَّة جَمِيلَة وَوَاسِعَة.
questions: Did she teach the dual (خَالَانِ / خَالَتَانِ) as a rule, or did it just turn up in a sentence? It changes whether I drill it or only explain it.
The days — did she give them bare (الأَحَد) or with يَوْم in front (يَوْمَ الأَحَدِ)?
Was the passage about Samer read aloud in class, and is reading aloud what she expects next week?
Was the weather set (ثَلْج، مَطَر، سَحَاب) a real topic or an aside off ثَلْج?
What did she set as homework?
